title: OpenCart Review (2026)
intro: OpenCart is evaluated here as an open-source commerce platform (plugin/core + extensions) — OpenCart is a GPL open-source PHP ecommerce platform. The primary path is a free core download plus hosting and extension TCO you own. Secondary sources cite optional managed OpenCart cloud around ~$59–$99/mo — treat as medium confidence and confirm live; SoftwareGlimpse does not invent first-party cloud tiles. Landscape open-source peer — WooCommerce keeps the cluster award (8.1). Research grounded 2026-08-18. This review uses SoftwareGlimpse’s Ecommerce methodology (ease of use, storefront/commerce fit, catalog & order depth, checkout conversion, integrations, omnichannel/POS, scalability, value, AI), scoring products inside their job cluster rather than against unrelated peers. It is based on first-party research, not hands-on lab testing.
summary: Choose OpenCart when you want a free PHP open-source cart and will own hosting and extensions — not when you need WordPress-native WooCommerce or hosted SaaS simplicity.
verdict: Choose OpenCart when you want a free PHP open-source cart and will own hosting and extensions — not when you need WordPress-native WooCommerce or hosted SaaS simplicity. Consider WooCommerce for WordPress-native open source; PrestaShop for EU commerce-first PHP; Magento for deeper B2B/enterprise; Shopify for hosted SaaS. Scores reflect first-party documentation as of 2026-08-17 — not hands-on product testing. Confirm current packaging, minimums and usage rates on the vendor site before purchase.

criterionAssessments.rationale: More approachable than Magento for simple PHP stores; still self-hosted ops versus Shopify/Woo guided paths.
Core job is open-source storefront. Landscape peer — WooCommerce keeps the open-source cluster award (8.1).
Solid catalog and order basics for SMB PHP carts; weaker than Magento for complex B2B programmes.
Checkout works via payment extensions; conversion quality depends on theme and gateway work.
Extension marketplace covers common payments and shipping — narrower mindshare than WooCommerce.
Not a retail POS product — in-person selling is extension territory at best.
Fine for SMB catalogs; high-GMV complex programmes usually outgrow classic OpenCart stacks.
Free GPL core is strong when you accept hosting/extension TCO and do not need Magento depth.
Minimal first-party AI versus modern SaaS platforms.

bestFor: SMB merchants wanting a free PHP open-source cart
Teams comfortable self-hosting and buying extensions
Catalogs that do not need Magento/Adobe programme depth
notIdealFor: Founders wanting zero hosting ops (see Shopify)
Retailers whose center of gravity is POS hardware
pros: Commerce-first PHP cart (not a CMS plugin)
Low license floor for self-hosted SMBs
cons: Managed cloud pricing needs live confirmation
limitations: Hosting, security, and extension TCO are on you even when the license is $0
Managed cloud floors are not first-party confirmed here — confirm live before budgeting
POS / omnichannel is extension-dependent, not a native retail bundle
Admin UX and ecosystem mindshare trail WooCommerce and Magento for many buyers
pricingSummary: Open-source core: free license + hosting/extension TCO. Optional managed cloud sometimes cited ~$59–$99/mo (confirm live — not first-party confirmed here). Confirm on opencart.com.
whoShouldChoose: Choose OpenCart when you want a free PHP open-source cart and will own hosting and extensions — not when you need WordPress-native WooCommerce or hosted SaaS simplicity.
whoShouldConsiderAlternatives: Consider WooCommerce for WordPress-native open source; PrestaShop for EU commerce-first PHP; Magento for deeper B2B/enterprise; Shopify for hosted SaaS.
